vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to the great outdoors, which is why he became a park ranger. But it was his time as a civilian in a war zone that changed him forever. He remembers the day vividly - the sound of gunfire, the smell of smoke, and the sight of flames engulfing a nearby building. Kofi had been forced to take shelter in a ditch, watching as people ran for their lives. The image of a young girl, no more than ten years old, being pulled from the rubble, haunts him still. After returning home, Kofi found it difficult to adjust. He would often find himself becoming easily irritated, particularly when his colleagues or friends tried to offer criticism or correction. It wasn't just the words themselves, but the tone and condescending manner in which they were delivered that set him off. "You're not listening," he would think to himself, "you don't understand what I've been through." As a result, Kofi began to isolate himself completely, cutting off contact with friends and family. He stopped attending social gatherings, and his only interactions were limited to his work as a park ranger. Being in nature, which was once a source of comfort for him, now served as a painful reminder of the traumatic event. The sounds of birds chirping or the rustling of leaves would transport him back to that ditch, reliving the fear and helplessness he felt. Kofi tried to avoid these triggers by taking on desk work, but even that proved challenging. The sight of military or police uniforms, which were a common occurrence in his line of work, would send his mind racing. To cope with his emotions, Kofi turned to substance use - drinking alcohol and taking medication to numb the pain. He would often find himself scrolling through news articles about the war zone, searching for answers as to why he had survived while others did not. This sense of survival guilt weighed heavily on him, making him feel isolated and set apart from others. As time went on, Kofi's sleep problems worsened. He would lie awake at night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. Even when he knew he was safe, he couldn't shake the feeling that something bad was lurking just beneath the surface. This hypervigilance extended to everyday situations - if a task took longer than expected, Kofi's anxiety would spike, and he would assume something terrible had happened. Kofi also struggled with feelings of having acted in ways that went against his values during the traumatic event. He couldn't shake the memory of not being able to help more people, and this sense of violation continued to haunt him. Despite his best efforts to avoid these triggers, Kofi found himself unable to escape them entirely. One day, while working at the park, he witnessed a controlled burn - flames engulfing a nearby area. The smell of smoke transported him back to that fateful day, and Kofi knew he needed help. He couldn't continue living in a state of constant hypervigilance, unable to relax or connect with others. It was this realization that brought Kofi to seek professional help. As he sits in the therapist's office, he is met with a sense of trepidation - what will happen if he opens up about his experiences? Will he be judged or criticized? But more than anything, Kofi hopes to find a way to silence the voices of self-doubt and guilt that have plagued him for so long. He yearns to reconnect with others, to find a sense of peace in nature once again, and to learn to forgive himself for surviving.
